notes.html:
Domain 7: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement (7%)

What the exam tests

Helping engineering teams adopt Claude (typically via Claude Code) safely and consistently: shared configuration, permissions, automation and rollout.

7.1 Project guidance: CLAUDE.md

A Markdown file Claude Code reads at the start of sessions for project conventions. - Locations (hierarchy): organisation/managed policy → project ./CLAUDE.md (commit to Git, shared) → user ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (personal) → sub-folder files for local rules. - Put in it: build/test/lint commands, architecture overview, code style, naming, "do/don't" rules, where things live, PR conventions. - Keep it concise and current; it is context on every session (long files dilute). - Shared in repo = consistent behaviour across the team.

7.2 Settings and permissions

  • .claude/settings.json → shared project settings (commit); .claude/settings.local.json → personal, not committed; user-level and managed (enterprise) settings also exist; managed policy can enforce rules.
  • Permission rules: allow (run without asking), ask, deny for tools/commands/paths, e.g. allow npm test, deny reading .env or running rm -rf, deny network tools in CI.
  • Principle: least privilege, deny sensitive paths, allow only safe repeatable commands; require review for the rest.
  • Modes: ask-per-action (default), plan mode (propose first), auto-accept edits: choose by risk.

7.3 Hooks, commands, subagents, MCP

Feature Purpose
Hooks Run your scripts at lifecycle events (e.g. before/after a tool runs) to enforce rules deterministically: run linter/tests, block edits to protected files, scan for secrets
Slash commands Saved prompts the team shares (e.g. /review, /release-notes)
Subagents Specialised assistants with own context and tool limits (e.g. security-reviewer)
MCP servers Connect issue trackers, docs, databases; project-scoped config shared via .mcp.json
Key idea (links back to Domain 4): hooks/permissions enforce; CLAUDE.md guides.

7.4 Automation and CI

  • Headless/non-interactive mode (e.g. claude -p "…") for scripts and CI: structured output, no human at the keyboard.
  • GitHub Actions integration for PR review/triage/issue-to-PR.
  • CI safety: least-privilege token, no production credentials, sandboxed runner, restricted tool allow-list, human review before merge, log outputs, spend limits.
  • Validate any generated code with tests, linters, SAST, dependency checks like any other contribution.

7.5 Rollout and enablement

  1. Pilot with willing team; baseline metrics.
  2. Provide starter CLAUDE.md, settings, command library, and a short training (what it's good/bad at, security rules).
  3. Champions + support channel; share prompts that work.
  4. Measure: cycle time, PR throughput/size, review time, test pass rate, defect escape, developer satisfaction, cost per developer. Beware vanity metrics (lines of code).
  5. Governance: approved plans/data policies, secret handling, code-review standards, licence/IP checks.
  6. Iterate configuration as the team learns.

7.6 Documentation as enablement

Good README, architecture notes, runbooks and test instructions help humans and Claude. Treat docs as part of the product.

Scenario

A 40-developer team wants consistent, safe Claude Code use, with CI PR reviews. - Commit CLAUDE.md (commands, conventions) + .claude/settings.json (allow test/lint; deny .env, deploy scripts). - Hook: run formatter and secret-scan after edits. - Shared /review command and security-reviewer subagent. - CI: PR-review job with read-only token, no prod secrets; humans approve merges. - Pilot with 8 devs for 3 weeks; track review time and defect rate; then expand.

Exam traps

  • ❌ Giving CI/headless runs production credentials or broad permissions.
  • ❌ Relying on CLAUDE.md text alone to enforce security (use permissions/hooks).
  • ❌ Each dev with different, uncommitted guidance.
  • ✅ Shared committed config; least-privilege permissions; hooks for enforcement; staged rollout with metrics.

Self-check

Q1. Shared vs personal settings files?

.claude/settings.json shared (committed); settings.local.json personal.

Q2. Guide vs enforce?

CLAUDE.md guides; permissions and hooks enforce.

Q3. Safe CI posture?

Least-privilege token, sandbox, allow-listed tools, no prod secrets, human merge approval.

CCAR-P cheat sheet

63 q · 120 min · $175 · 720/1000 scaled · scenario/consulting style

Domain (weight) Core ideas
Integration 19% MCP · least privilege · secrets managers · RAG (chunking, hybrid, rerank, ACL at retrieval) · idempotent retries + backoff
Design 17% Single call → workflow → agent → multi-agent: simplest that works. Success criteria first.

  1. Biggest model for everything
  2. Agent where a workflow works
  3. Compliance via prompt wording
  4. "Add more context" for a retrieval problem

Elimination order

Simplest design → enforced control → least privilege → measure before changing → HITL for high-risk.

questions.question: An agent needs to read customer records and update orders. Which permission design is best?

options.A: Let the model decide its own permissions
options.B: Embed API keys in the system prompt
options.C: Least-privilege, scoped credentials; read-only by default, writes gated
options.D: One admin credential shared by all tools

questions.explanation: Least privilege, with gated write actions.

questions.question: Where should API secrets be handled?

options.D: In a secrets manager/environment, never in model context or repos

questions.explanation: Secrets never go through prompts or code.

questions.question: A RAG assistant gives wrong answers; logs show the correct passage was never retrieved. What should you fix?

options.B: Add more context to the prompt

questions.explanation: Diagnose retrieval vs model; here retrieval failed.

questions.question: Select TWO controls that correctly enforce per-user data access in RAG.

options.B: Tell the model not to reveal restricted docs
options.C: Filter by the user's permissions before content enters context
options.D: Apply document-level access control at retrieval time

questions.explanation: Enforcement belongs in the retrieval layer, not the prompt.

questions.question: A write-action tool call times out; retrying may duplicate the order. Best design?

options.B: Let the model guess the result
options.C: Use idempotency keys with backoff and surface failures clearly

questions.explanation: Idempotency + backoff makes retries safe.

questions.question: Why does MCP matter when integrating many internal systems?

options.A: It removes the need for permissions
options.C: A standard protocol to expose tools/data reduces bespoke glue and enables reuse

questions.explanation: Standardised tool/data connectivity.

questions.question: A task has fixed, known steps and needs reliability. What is the best architecture?
questions.explanation: Known steps → workflow; use the simplest pattern that meets the need.

questions.question: When does a multi-agent design make most sense?

options.C: When subtasks are parallel/independent or need isolated contexts and the benefit outweighs cost and coordination risk
options.D: When there is no time to design

questions.explanation: Multi-agent adds cost and failure modes; justify it.

questions.question: A client asks for 'an agent' to extract 5 fields from invoices. Best recommendation?

options.A: A single structured LLM call (possibly a small model) with schema validation

questions.explanation: Simplest design that meets the requirement.

questions.question: Before proposing an architecture, you should first:

options.D: Agree measurable success criteria and constraints with the stakeholders

questions.explanation: Discovery and success criteria come first.

questions.question: Which grader is best for validating that output is valid JSON matching a schema?
questions.explanation: Objective, verifiable checks → code graders.

questions.question: You introduce an LLM-as-judge for tone. What must you do?

options.B: Provide a clear rubric and calibrate against human labels
options.D: Use the same model without a rubric

questions.explanation: Calibrate judges against human ratings.

questions.question: After a prompt change, overall score rises but one customer segment drops. Best action?

options.C: Analyse by segment, investigate the regression, then decide

questions.explanation: Segmented analysis and regression testing.

questions.question: Select TWO elements of a good eval dataset.

options.D: Cases added from real production failures

questions.explanation: Representative + edge + production-derived failures.

questions.question: A hospital requires that Claude never exposes PHI to unauthorised staff. Best approach?

options.C: Implement access controls, filtering and audit logging in the system; BAA with the vendor; plus HITL where needed
options.D: Add 'never share PHI' to the system prompt

questions.explanation: Compliance needs real controls, not a line in the prompt.

questions.question: Which action should always have human approval?

options.D: Issuing refunds above a defined threshold or other irreversible financial actions

questions.explanation: High-impact irreversible actions need approval gates.

questions.question: A prompt-injection incident is detected in production. Correct sequence?

options.C: Contain (revoke/kill switch) → investigate logs → remediate → notify as required → add cases to evals

questions.explanation: Standard incident response, feeding learnings back to evals.

questions.question: The client wants to start building immediately. You lack baselines and success metrics. Best response?

options.C: Run discovery: define goals, baseline, success criteria and risks first

questions.explanation: Skipping discovery is a classic anti-pattern.

questions.question: How should you explain a trade-off between accuracy and cost to a business sponsor?

options.B: Express it in business terms (risk, cost, time, value) with options and a recommendation

questions.explanation: Translate technical trade-offs into business impact.

questions.question: A prompt change will go to production. Which lifecycle practice applies?

options.B: Version it, regression-test against evals, gated release with rollback plan

questions.explanation: Change control for prompts/models/tools.

questions.question: Which statement about model selection is correct?

options.C: Always use the most powerful model
options.D: Choose by capability, cost and speed, justified by evals; smaller models often suffice

questions.explanation: Right-size the model to the task.

questions.question: An app sends the same 20k-token policy document with every request. Best optimisation?

options.B: Use prompt caching with the stable prefix first

questions.explanation: Cache the static prefix to cut cost and latency.

questions.question: Answers are poor because the model is given 50 loosely related chunks. Best fix?

options.A: Improve retrieval/reranking so only relevant context is included

questions.explanation: Context engineering: relevance over volume.

questions.question: Which is the safest practice for Claude in a shared CI pipeline?

options.B: Give it production credentials for convenience
options.D: Least-privilege permissions, allow-listed commands, sandboxed runner, review before merge

questions.explanation: Safe permissions in shared/CI environments.

questions.question: A team wants consistent Claude behaviour on a repository. Best approach?

options.C: Each dev writes their own prompts
options.D: Commit shared project guidance/settings and keep personal prefs local

questions.explanation: Shared, versioned project settings.

questions.question: Two MCP tools both read 'customer data' and have near-identical descriptions; the agent keeps picking the wrong one. Best fix?

options.C: Rewrite the tool descriptions to be distinct and precise, or merge the tools

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions drive selection; ambiguity causes misuse.

questions.question: A third-party API returns 429 errors during peak load. Best handling?

options.A: Exponential backoff with jitter, plus rate limiting or queueing on your side
options.B: Retry instantly in a tight loop
options.D: Let the model invent a response

questions.explanation: Backoff and rate management protect both systems.

questions.question: Which RAG change most directly helps both keyword-specific and semantic queries?

options.D: Hybrid search (keyword plus embeddings) with reranking

questions.explanation: Hybrid search plus reranking improves recall and precision.

questions.question: A tool call fails. What should the agent do with the failure?

options.D: Surface the error clearly and handle it

questions.explanation: Failures must be visible and handled safely.

questions.question: Select TWO secure ways to give an integration its credentials.

options.B: Commit the key to the repo
options.D: Secrets manager with scoped, rotating credentials

questions.explanation: Keep secrets out of model context and repos; scope and rotate.

questions.question: An internal knowledge base is updated hourly. What matters most for RAG correctness?

options.B: Freshness: re-indexing or incremental updates with versioning

questions.explanation: Stale indexes produce stale answers.

questions.question: Requirement: classify inbound emails into 6 categories at high volume and low cost. Best design?

options.D: Single call to a small model with a strict schema, validated by an eval set

questions.explanation: Simplest viable design wins.

questions.question: Open-ended research tasks with an unpredictable number of steps. Which pattern fits?

options.B: An agent with defined tools, limits and checkpoints

questions.explanation: Unpredictable paths justify an agent, with guardrails.

questions.question: A task's parts are independent and each needs a large separate context. Best structure?

options.C: Orchestrator with parallel sub-agents, aggregating results
options.D: One agent doing all sequentially in one context

questions.explanation: Context isolation and parallelism justify subagents.

questions.question: Which is a real downside of multi-agent systems?

options.C: Higher token cost and added coordination failure modes
options.D: They remove the need for evals

questions.explanation: Multi-agent adds cost and complexity.

questions.question: A client wants a nightly bulk summarisation of 200k documents, no urgency. What optimisation fits?

options.A: Batch processing, possibly with prompt caching

questions.explanation: Non-urgent bulk work suits batch for cost savings.

questions.question: Select TWO design elements that make an agent safer to run.
questions.explanation: Limits and approvals bound risk.

questions.question: Before choosing between workflow and agent, what do you need?

options.A: Clear requirements and success criteria, including risk and latency needs

questions.explanation: Requirements drive architecture.

questions.question: You need to check that a generated SQL query returns the expected rows. Best grader?

options.B: Code-based: execute against a test database and compare

questions.explanation: Executable, objective checks beat judgement here.

questions.question: A summarisation app's quality is subjective. Which approach scales best?

options.D: LLM-as-judge with a rubric, calibrated on a human-labelled sample

questions.explanation: Calibrated LLM judges scale subjective grading.

questions.question: Production users report a new failure type. Best use of it?

options.B: Add it to the eval set and regression-test fixes

questions.explanation: Production failures should feed the eval dataset.

questions.question: Quality dropped after switching model versions. What process would have caught it?

options.C: Running the regression eval suite before release

questions.explanation: Evals gate model/prompt changes.

questions.question: Select TWO signs a metric is well chosen.

options.A: It ties to the business outcome

questions.explanation: Good metrics are tied to value and measurable reliably.

questions.question: Aggregate accuracy is 92% but one high-value segment is at 60%. Right reading?

options.C: The aggregate hides a serious segment problem

questions.explanation: Segment analysis reveals hidden failures.

questions.question: A bank requires an audit trail for every AI-assisted decision. Best control?

options.D: Log inputs, outputs, tool calls and approver identity immutably

questions.explanation: Auditability needs real logging infrastructure.

questions.question: Where should output moderation for a public chatbot sit?

options.A: As a separate validation layer in code that checks responses before display

questions.explanation: Guardrails belong in enforced layers.

questions.question: Under GDPR-style principles, which practice is most aligned?

options.D: Data minimisation: send only the personal data the task needs

questions.explanation: Minimisation and purpose limitation.

questions.question: A vendor will process PHI. What is required before proceeding (HIPAA context)?

options.B: A business associate agreement and appropriate safeguards

questions.explanation: BAAs are required for vendors handling PHI.

questions.question: An agent can send external emails. Which control is most appropriate?

options.A: Human approval or strict allow-lists before sending
options.D: Rely on a polite system prompt

questions.explanation: Gate externally visible irreversible actions.

questions.question: Select TWO incident-response steps after discovering an agent leaked data.

options.A: Investigate using logs and notify as required
options.C: Contain: revoke credentials or disable the tool
options.D: Wait to see if it repeats

questions.explanation: Contain, investigate, and notify; preserve evidence.

questions.question: A sponsor says 'just make it work like magic'. First step?

options.C: Run discovery to translate goals into measurable success criteria and constraints

questions.explanation: Discovery and measurable criteria come first.

questions.question: Legal is worried about data risk and is blocking the project. Best approach?

options.C: Engage early, show controls and evidence, and propose a staged scope

questions.explanation: Collaborate and evidence controls.

questions.question: How should a pilot be structured?

options.C: Defined scope, success metrics and exit criteria agreed upfront

questions.explanation: Pilots need measurable exit criteria.

questions.question: The model provider announces a deprecation. How should this be treated?

options.B: As a surprise to react to later
options.C: As a planned change: assess, test with evals, schedule migration and rollback
options.D: As a reason to cancel evals

questions.explanation: Plan model lifecycle changes.

questions.question: Which is the best way to present options to executives?

options.C: 2–3 options with trade-offs in cost, risk and value, plus a recommendation

questions.explanation: Business-term trade-offs and a recommendation.

questions.question: Select TWO lifecycle practices after release.
questions.explanation: Operate and improve continuously.

questions.question: A support bot is slow and costly because every request resends a long static policy. Best fix?

options.D: Prompt caching with the static content at the start of the prompt

questions.explanation: Cache the stable prefix.

questions.question: For reliable multi-step math or logic, which technique helps?

options.C: Chain-of-thought or extended thinking, validated by checks

questions.explanation: Reasoning techniques improve multi-step accuracy.

questions.question: Which prompt layout is generally better with a very long document?

options.D: Place the document first, with the question and instructions after it

questions.explanation: Long content first, clear delimiters, then the ask.

questions.question: Select TWO benefits of few-shot examples.
questions.explanation: Examples steer format and style, not guarantee truth.

questions.question: A chat agent's history grows until quality degrades. Best context technique?

options.C: Summarise or compact history and retrieve details just in time

questions.explanation: Context management prevents dilution.

questions.question: Which hook-style practice best enforces code-quality rules in team workflows?

options.C: Automated checks (lint, tests, secret scanning) run as hooks or CI gates

questions.explanation: Enforce with automation, not only instructions.

questions.question: A new team is adopting Claude for engineering. Best rollout step?

options.C: Pilot with a small group, gather feedback and measure usage and cost
options.D: Mandate for all on day one

questions.explanation: Staged rollout with feedback and monitoring.

docs.html:
Exam facts and the deadline problem

Key facts (both exams)

  • Delivered by Pearson VUE: OnVUE (online) or test centre. English and Japanese.
  • Scaled score 720 / 1000 to pass. This is not 72% correct.
  • Multiple-response ("Select TWO"): assume no partial credit.
  • No negative marking: never leave a question blank.
  • Closed book. No AI tools, no browser translation.
  • Valid 12 months; renewal via a free non-proctored assessment on the Partner Academy. Lapse = full exam again.
  • Retakes: wait 14 days (after 1st fail), 30 days (2nd), 90 days (3rd). Max 4 attempts per rolling 12 months. Full fee each time.
  • Must be 18+, government photo ID, name must match Pearson profile exactly.
  • Registration needs a company email on a partner-registered domain (you have this via your partner access).
  • Reschedule/cancel at least 48 h before, otherwise the fee is lost.

⚠️ 7 December 2026 content update

Anthropic is updating CCAO-F, CCDV-F and CCAR-P content from 7 Dec 2026. New exam guides are expected on 17 Nov 2026.

Your deadline is 11 Dec, so there are two paths:

Path When to sit Study from Risk
A. Old blueprint Book on or before 6 Dec Current guide (notes in this repo) Compressed timeline (~4 weeks). A failed attempt on 6 Dec means a 14-day wait, so no retake before 11 Dec
B. New blueprint Book 7–10 Dec New guide from 17 Nov + this repo's fundamentals Unknown changes; little practice material exists yet

Recommendation: Aim to sit both exams around 1–5 Dec. When the new guide lands on 17 Nov, diff it against ccao-f/notes and ccar-p/notes and patch gaps. If you aren't ready by ~3 Dec, you're deliberately on Path B.

A retake needs a 14-day gap, so book the first attempt early (ideally by ~25 Nov) to leave any buffer at all. Pearson slots can fill.

Which exam first?

CCAO-F is generally reported as the easiest of the four. CCAR-P is judgement/consulting-heavy, with fewer obscure-config questions than CCAR-F. Do CCAO-F first; its material (prompting, governance, evaluation, model choice) overlaps with CCAR-P domains 4 and 6.

docs.title: 4-week plan (6 Nov → 6 Dec), both exams
docs.html:
4-week plan (6 Nov → 6 Dec), both exams

~1.5–2 h on weekdays, ~3 h on weekends. Adjust to your experience.

Week 1 (6–12 Nov): Foundations + CCAO-F core

  • Mon–Tue: Download both official Exam Guide PDFs; read docs/00. Book exam slots. Skim the Partner Academy CCAO-F learning path.
  • Wed–Fri: ccao-f/notes ch. 1–4 (evaluation, verification, workflow design).
  • Weekend: ch. 5–6 (governance, prompting). Flashcards ccao-f.csv (first pass).

Week 2 (13–19 Nov): CCAO-F finish + CCAR-P start

  • 17 Nov: new exam guides publish. Diff them against these notes.
  • Mon–Tue: ch. 7–9 (product/model selection, config, troubleshooting).
  • Wed: CCAO-F practice: quiz.py ccao-f -n 30, log weak areas.
  • Thu–Sun: ccar-p/notes domains 1 and 2 (36% of the exam).

Week 3 (20–26 Nov): CCAR-P depth

  • Domains 3, 4, 5 (evaluation, governance, stakeholders; 44%).
  • Domains 6, 7 (models/prompting/context; developer productivity).
  • Build something: a small RAG + MCP project with an eval set (even a toy). The exam asks why, not how.
  • Weekend: quiz.py ccar-p -n 25 twice; review every wrong answer.

Week 4 (27 Nov – 6 Dec): Test-taking

  • Full timed simulations: 60 q / 120 min (CCAO-F), 63 q / 120 min (CCAR-P).
  • Last 2 days: cheat sheets, weak domains only, exam-day checklist.
  • Run the OnVUE system test on the exact machine and network you'll use.
  • Sit exams (CCAO-F first, CCAR-P a few days later).

Rules of thumb

  • Two passes of every flashcard deck before simulations.
  • Don't leave a domain until you can explain why each wrong option is wrong.
  • Score ≥ 80% on your own practice before booking the real thing.

Where each resource fits

  • Notes (Study tab): read one chapter → do its self-check → domain quiz in Learn mode.
  • Glossary (Guides & glossary): skim daily; every term should feel familiar.
  • CCAR-P case studies: attempt each before opening the model answer. Do 2 per week from week 2.
  • Hands-on project: schedule a weekend in week 3. Even a partial build helps a lot.
  • Learn more links: at the end of every chapter; open the Anthropic docs pages for the topics you score lowest on.

docs.title: Auto-update: how it works and how to switch it on
docs.html:
Auto-update: how it works and how to switch it on

What happens automatically

  1. Daily watcher (.github/workflows/watch-anthropic.yml, 03:17 UTC) fetches the pages in sources.json (Anthropic news, Partner Academy certification pages, FAQ, eligibility, Claude models page).
  2. If a page's text changed it saves a diff in state/changes/, adds a line to the site's changelog, opens a GitHub issue labelled exam-update, rebuilds the site and redeploys it.
  3. The website's Update button (top right) shows a red dot when a newer version is live. Click it to see the changelog and watcher status, then Install the new content. Your progress is untouched.

One-time setup (5 minutes)

  1. Push this repo to GitHub (branch main).
  2. Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions. Your site appears at https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/.
  3. Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions: Read and write, and tick Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests.
  4. (Optional, for AI-drafted updates) Settings → Secrets → Actions → ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
  5. Run Actions → Watch Anthropic for exam updates → Run workflow once to save the baseline.

Getting new official material in (the important part)

The Partner Academy (Skilljar) needs your company login, so a bot cannot download the Exam Guide PDF. When the new guides appear (17 Nov 2026): 1. Download the CCAO-F and CCAR-P guide PDFs while logged in. 2. Drop them into inbox/ and push. The AI draft update workflow reads them and opens a pull request containing: - ai-reports/<date>-<exam>.md: what changed (domains, weights, scope, rules) and which notes need edits - questions/pending/<exam>-<date>.json: draft original questions 3. Review against the guide. Fix the notes in ccao-f/notes / ccar-p/notes. Publish good draft questions with python scripts/approve_pending.py questions/pending/<file>.json. Merge → the site redeploys → click Update.

No API key? Skip step 2 and edit the notes by hand; the deploy/update flow is the same.

Limits (be aware)

  • Page watching detects that something changed, not what it means. Nothing is merged without you.
  • AI-drafted questions can be wrong. They stay in pending/ until you approve them.
  • The watcher can't see content behind the Skilljar login; it records those pages as "login required".
  • Don't put real exam questions (brain dumps) in this repo. That breaches the exam agreement.

Run locally

pip install markdown pypdf
python scripts/build_site.py          # regenerate site/data/content.json
python3 -m http.server -d site 8000   # open http://localhost:8000
python scripts/watch_sources.py       # run the watcher by hand

docs.title: CCAR-P case studies: practise the thinking
docs.html:
CCAR-P case studies: practise the thinking

For each: read the situation, decide your answer, then open the model answer.

Case 1: "We need an agent!"

Situation: A logistics firm wants to read supplier emails and put the order number, ship date and quantity into their ERP. ~30k emails/day, 3 email templates plus free text. Errors must be <2%. Latency isn't critical.

Model answer

Design: workflow, not an agent. Small/mid model, structured output (schema), code validation (date/quantity formats, order exists in ERP), low-confidence → human queue, nightly batch for backlog. Why: steps are fixed and verifiable; an agent adds cost and unpredictability. Controls: write to ERP via a scoped service account with idempotency keys; audit log. Evals: 1,000 labelled emails incl. edge cases; track per-field accuracy and segment by template/language; gate release at agreed threshold. Rejected: multi-agent (unneeded), real-time streaming (not required), prompt-only validation.

Case 2: The leaky knowledge assistant

Situation: An HR RAG assistant sometimes shows salary data to managers who shouldn't see it. The team proposes adding "never reveal salary of other teams" to the system prompt.

Model answer

Reject prompt-only fix. Enforce document-level access control at retrieval: filter the index by the asking user's entitlements (pass identity through), so restricted chunks never enter the context. Add output scanning, audit logs, and adversarial tests (injection asking for salaries). Add these cases to the eval suite. Why: prompts can be bypassed; compliance needs enforced controls.

Case 3: Bad answers: model or retrieval?

Situation: A support bot answers 70% correctly. Stakeholders say "use the biggest model".

Model answer

Diagnose first. Take 100 failures; classify: right chunk not retrieved vs retrieved-but-misused vs source wrong/stale vs format. If retrieval misses dominate → hybrid search, reranking, better chunking, contextual retrieval, metadata filters. If misuse → clearer prompt/few-shot examples. Only test a bigger model via the eval suite, comparing quality vs cost. Why: measuring locates the cause; "bigger model" is an untested, costly guess.

Case 4: Cost blow-up

Situation: A contract Q&A tool sends a 40-page contract plus a 5k-token instruction set with every question. Users ask ~10 questions per contract. Bills are high; responses slow.

Model answer

Prompt caching: put instructions + contract first (static prefix, marked for caching), the question last. Subsequent questions hit the cache (cheaper reads, lower latency) within the TTL. Consider retrieving relevant clauses if contracts are huge. Keep eval baseline to confirm no quality loss. If bulk offline analysis is needed, use batch. Rejected: shortening instructions blindly, switching to the smallest model without evals.

Case 5: Autonomous finance agent

Situation: The CFO wants an agent that reconciles invoices and pays suppliers automatically.

Model answer

Agent/workflow may prepare reconciliation, but payments are irreversible and high-impact → human approval gate (and dual control above a threshold). Least-privilege tools (read vs payment separated), idempotency keys, spend caps, full audit trail, anomaly alerts, kill switch. Start with shadow mode (suggest only), compare to humans, then graduated autonomy for low-value, low-risk categories. Messaging: autonomy earned with evidence, not granted up front.

Case 6: Regulator and the clinical summariser

Situation: A health provider wants Claude to summarise patient notes. Compliance asks "how do we prove HIPAA compliance?"

Model answer

Map requirements → controls → evidence: BAA with vendor; approved environment; role-based access and retrieval filtering by treating relationship; minimum-necessary inputs/de-identification where possible; audit logs of access; output labelled AI-generated with clinician verification; incident runbook; periodic access reviews and red-team tests. Provide a control matrix and logs as evidence.

Case 7: Upgrading the model

Situation: A newer model version is available and the old one will be deprecated in 6 months.

Model answer

Planned change: run full eval suite on the new model (quality, cost, latency, safety); examine segment regressions; adjust prompts/examples; canary (e.g. 5–10% traffic) with monitoring; keep rollback; communicate dates; update documentation and cost forecasts. Make model IDs configuration, not hard-coded.

Case 8: Team adoption of Claude Code

Situation: 60 developers; leadership wants "AI everywhere" and plans to give CI full repo and cloud credentials so Claude can "fix things automatically".

Model answer

Pilot first; commit CLAUDE.md + shared settings with deny rules for secrets; hooks for lint/tests/secret scanning; CI uses read-only, least-privilege tokens, no production credentials, sandboxed runners; Claude proposes PRs, humans approve merges. Track review time, defects, cost per dev; expand by evidence.

Hands-on project: Policy Q&A with RAG + MCP + evals (≈ 3 hours)

Building this once makes CCAR-P scenario questions intuitive. You do not need to finish it perfectly.

Goal

A command-line assistant that answers questions about a small set of company policy documents, with citations, access control, a tool exposed over MCP, and a test set that scores quality.

Prerequisites

Python 3.10+, an Anthropic API key (console.anthropic.com), ~10 text/markdown "policy" files you write yourself (leave, expenses, security, etc.), each tagged with an access level (public or hr-only).

Step 1: Ingest and chunk

  1. Split each file by headings into 200-500-token chunks.
  2. Store for each chunk: text, source, section, access_level, updated_at.
  3. Learning point: keep the section title with each chunk so retrieval has context.

Step 2: Index with hybrid search

  1. Build a keyword index (BM25, e.g. rank_bm25) and a vector index (any embedding provider + a small local store).
  2. Retrieve top 20 from each, merge, optionally rerank to the best 5.
  3. Learning point: try an exact-code query ("Policy HR-204") and a paraphrase query; see why hybrid helps.

Step 3: Enforce access at retrieval

Add a user_role parameter; filter chunks by access_level before ranking. Test: a public user asking about salary bands must get "not found". Learning point: access control belongs in retrieval, not in the prompt.

Step 4: Generate with citations

Prompt: answer only from the provided chunks in <documents>; cite [source §section]; say "not found" if absent. Use low temperature. Static instructions first, retrieved chunks and question last (cache-friendly).

Step 5: Expose a tool via MCP

Create a small MCP server (Python SDK) with one read-only tool search_policies(query) returning top chunks with metadata. Connect it to Claude Desktop or Claude Code and ask questions. Learning point: tool description quality drives correct tool use; keep it read-only; never put secrets in tool output.

Step 6: Build the eval set

Write 30 test cases in JSON: question, expected facts, expected source, role. Include 5 edge cases (not in docs), 5 adversarial (injection inside a policy file, "ignore rules"), 5 access-control tests. Graders: code-based (expected source cited? "not found" when it should be?) and an LLM-judge for faithfulness with a rubric. Check the judge against 10 hand-graded answers.

Step 7: Measure and improve (one change at a time)

Record baseline: retrieval recall@5, faithfulness, access-leak count (must be 0), cost, latency. Then try one change at a time: chunk size, reranking, few-shot examples, model tier, prompt caching. Keep a log of change → effect.

Step 8: Write a one-page architecture note

Diagram, trust boundaries, controls, known limitations, how a model upgrade would be rolled out. Practising this is excellent preparation for stakeholder questions.

Checklist: you can now explain

  • [ ] Why hybrid search + reranking beats embeddings alone
  • [ ] Why ACLs are enforced at retrieval
  • [ ] How tool descriptions affect behaviour
  • [ ] How you'd detect and fix a retrieval vs generation failure
  • [ ] Why evals gate every change

  • Contextual Retrieval: https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval
  • Anthropic Cookbook (examples incl. RAG & evals): https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cookbook
